statements.quote: This newsletter’s author is a psychiatrist, who is saying goodbye to “medication management” as part of his practice.
statements.context: Opening of the Olanzapine installment in the author's farewell-to-meds series. The author (Owen Muir) states he is dropping medication management from his own clinical practice to focus on neuromodulation, and is writing a series of medication essays as he makes that change.
statements.note: Author's own practice plan (CONTROL candidate); borderline, present-progressive statement of a decision in progress.

statements.quote: Neuromodulation is the future of the field
statements.context: Same opening paragraph of the Olanzapine post. After saying he is leaving medication management, the author asserts that neuromodulation (TMS and related device-based treatments) is the future of psychiatry, and that his own daily practice now focuses on it.
statements.note: Broad trend call with no date or metric; restates the author's recurring neuromodulation-first thesis.

statements.quote: This was always a problem, and never going to be something that got to market at scale.
statements.context: About long-acting injectable (LAI) olanzapine, brand Zyprexa Relprevv. Its post-injection delirium sedation syndrome requires three hours of EKG-monitored observation at every monthly dose. The author says this made the LAI product never able to reach market scale, and he is shocked the maker rolled it out at all.
statements.note: Negative market call on LAI olanzapine; framed partly in past tense ('was always') but asserts it will never scale.

statements.quote: I was going to do a big long thing, like I do. I might still.
statements.context: Short Paxil (paroxetine) installment of the medication series. The author says he planned a long essay on Paxil, may still write one, but keeps this piece short because, like Paxil withdrawal, less is more.
statements.note: Trivial own-newsletter publishing intention; coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: Being a perfectionist means less practice, and less practice means my peak is less good than it will be tomorrow.
statements.context: Essay on why the author writes a daily newsletter. He explains his rule that something goes out every day and that more practice raises his writing peak; he expects his future peak to be better than today's.
statements.note: Personal-improvement statement, near-truism; low forecast value. Logged for recall.

statements.quote: Any one of those articles might get me in trouble.
statements.context: After listing his repeated satirical pieces attacking private equity (PE) in healthcare, the author says any one of them might cause him trouble with the companies named, but writing so much means most readers and targets do not read them all.
statements.note: Hedged personal-risk speculation; low forecast value. Logged for recall.

statements.quote: My friend Dave Chase has been writing about the coming apocalypse in liability for corporate America for a while ... I’m not a lawyer. But I can see the writing on the wall…and write about it.
statements.context: ERISA section of the daily-writing essay. The author restates Dave Chase's forecast of a coming liability apocalypse for corporate America from ERISA fiduciary lawsuits, citing lawyer Jerry Schlichter (2-0 at the Supreme Court, $600M+ retirement settlements) now targeting healthcare plans at firms such as Anthem, Target, T-Mobile, Walgreens and Lockheed Martin. The author endorses it: he can see the writing on the wall.
statements.confidence_phrase: I can see the writing on the wall
statements.note: Endorsed restatement of Dave Chase's third-party forecast; the Schlichter target list is quoted from Chase, not the author.

statements.quote: Alternatively, you can have class action lawyers and federal regulators dismantle the next decade of your fortune.
statements.context: Closing the ERISA section, the author addresses wealthy corporate decision-makers: either change health coverage to include mental health benefits that help people with psychiatric illness, or face class action lawyers and federal regulators dismantling the next decade of their fortune. Conditional call on ERISA fiduciary liability enforcement.
statements.note: Conditional and rhetorical (offered as a choice); implies ERISA class actions and federal enforcement against employer health plans over the next decade.

statements.quote: H4 receptor ligands may in the future be tested for neuroimmunological disorders and potentially neurodegenerative disorders in which inflammation plays a role, but clinical tests have not yet been initiated.
statements.context: Footnote 2 of the Remeron (mirtazapine) post, basic-science background on histamine receptors that the author says he will drop in a footnote. The text is quoted from a review paper, not written by the author. It says H4 receptor ligands may be tested in the future for neuroimmunological and neurodegenerative disorders.
statements.note: Quoted third-party review text in a footnote; author does not adopt or comment on it. Logged for recall.
